extracted.intended_audience: researchers and policy analysts studying notice-and-comment rulemaking, political scientists, and administrative law scholars who code and analyze public comments and agency responses
extracted.subtask_description: A coding scheme and methodological guidance for identifying commenter positions, coalition membership, organization types, asks, and measuring lobbying success and policy influence in notice-and-comment rulemaking. Includes recommendations for computational and qualitative methods and policy reforms to improve information quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: position (coding of comment stance)
rubrics_metrics.description: Code a comment's position on the main dimension of conflict using categorical codes: 1 = Opposed to the rule change for moving in the wrong direction; 2 = Opposed to the change, prefers no change though might accept some change; 3 = Supports the rule change but asking for less; 4 = Supports the rule change as is; 5 = Supports the rule change but asking for more; 6 = Opposed because the change does not go far enough; 0 = No position.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Code relative to the change from current policy (X1) to proposed policy (X2): what is the commenter's ideal point? Examples provided (e.g., supporting a deregulatory change means supporting the rule). Use the figure/ideal-point logic: positions 3-5 are closer to X2 than X1, etc. Include explicit examples and a rare code 6 for 'too little' objections.

rubrics_metrics.name: position_certainty
rubrics_metrics.description: Code how certain the coder is about the commenter's position: 1 = fairly certain (may also be left blank), 2 = unsure, 3 = totally unclear.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use when the comment's stance is ambiguous; leaving blank is allowed if fairly certain. This field captures coder confidence rather than commenter ambiguity alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: coalition_comment
rubrics_metrics.description: Indicator and label if the commentator is lobbying alongside other commenters in a way that suggests a coordinated coalition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If part of a coalition, enter the name of one main organization and use that for all compatible asks. Coalitions may be explicit (joint letters) or implicit (compatibly worded asks). Avoid artificially splitting essentially aligned interests just to create conflict; coalition detection should focus on the main dimension(s) of policy conflict.

rubrics_metrics.name: coalition_type
rubrics_metrics.description: Classify coalitions by whether they primarily represent public interest or private interests.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use 'public' if the coalition is primarily lobbying on behalf of some idea of the public interest; use 'private' if the coalition is mainly on behalf of private interests, even if they use public-interest language. The key distinction is whether lead organizations will profit from the coalition's advocacy.

rubrics_metrics.name: comment_type
rubrics_metrics.description: Categorize the comment's origin: 'org' (organization making substantive suggestions), 'elected' (comment from an elected official), 'individual' (personal capacity), 'corp campaign' (form letter used by many small businesses), or 'mass' (petition-like campaign).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For 'elected' add subtype (house, senate, governor, etc.). For 'mass' add subtypes: 'mass;grassroots' (genuine individual mobilization), 'mass;astroturf' (deceptive/paid mobilization, fake or non-consenting names), 'mass;corp campaign' (large number of businesses). Use cues like why people support and evidence of payment/deception to distinguish astroturf.

rubrics_metrics.name: org_name
rubrics_metrics.description: Standardized name of the organization when comment_type = 'org'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Revise algorithmic guesses to the clearest, standardized, unique version of the organization's name. If multiple orgs signed, prefer the main organizer (letterhead), or a previously seen org to aid linkage; if unclear, use the first signatory. Append '; coalition' to org_type if multiple orgs.

rubrics_metrics.name: org_type
rubrics_metrics.description: Classification of organization type using tags (examples include 'corp', 'corp group', 'gov', 'ngo', 'other') with semicolon-delimited subtypes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply semicolon subtypes like 'corp;small business', 'gov;state', 'ngo;advocacy', 'ngo;thinktank', 'ngo;union', 'ngo;ej' (environmental justice/frontline community). Some organizations may receive multiple semicolon tags. Code 501(c)(3)s that operate as industry associations as 'corp group' when appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: ask
rubrics_metrics.description: A concise text snippet (e.g., a sentence) that best captures the comment's overall ask or requested action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Extract the sentence or phrase that most clearly summarizes the comment's main request; for organizational comments this often mirrors the primary demand or objection.

rubrics_metrics.name: ask1/ask2/ask3 (top specific asks)
rubrics_metrics.description: Up to three specific asks or objections in the comment, each capturing a main issue the comment addresses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the comment touches multiple issues, select the top three distinct issues/asks (not merely the first three mentioned). Each ask should reflect a substantive requested change or objection, e.g., specific regulatory text to be changed or points opposed/supported.

rubrics_metrics.name: disaggregate_policies_into_multiple_dimensions
rubrics_metrics.description: When measuring lobbying success and positions, disaggregate a policy into multiple issues (dimensions of conflict) rather than reducing support/opposition to a single spatial dimension.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Refine coding by identifying multiple distinct reasons/claims within coalitions (e.g., tribal sovereignty vs. environmental concerns) and code coalition dynamics per dimension to avoid conflating distinct objections as a single 'opposed' category.

rubrics_metrics.name: large-scale_hand-coded_lobbying_success
rubrics_metrics.description: Measure lobbying success via large-scale, hand-coded indicators of position, coalition, and outcomes across many comments and rules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use manual coding to build datasets on positions and coalition alignment; recognize limits (loss of multidimensional conflict) and consider complementing with computational measures for robustness.

rubrics_metrics.name: detailed_case_studies / process_tracing
rubrics_metrics.description: Use detailed case studies and process-tracing methods to link inputs (comments), critical junctures, and outputs (rule changes), especially in rulemakings that span administrations or have clear lineage to prior rules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because rulemaking has structured inputs and outputs, process tracing is well-suited; prioritize cases that reverse or modify prior rules across administrations as strong candidates for causal inference.

rubrics_metrics.name: computational_measure_of_change_between_draft_and_final
rubrics_metrics.description: Use computational text comparison to measure change between draft and final rule text (e.g., percent of words changed, which words changed).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Link observed textual changes to commenter demands via text reuse methods, phrase matching, or other similarity measures. Challenges include attributing causality; use hybrid approaches (hand-coded anchors + automated matching).

rubrics_metrics.name: use_hand_coded_data_as_training_for_classifiers
rubrics_metrics.description: Leverage hand-coded lobbying coalitions and labeled data as training corpora for supervised machine learning classifiers to automatically detect lobbying coalitions and commenter positions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Trained classifiers may outperform unsupervised clustering. Ensure training data quality, and use classifiers to scale detection of coalitions across large corpora while validating against hand-coded samples.

rubrics_metrics.name: targeted_computational_analysis_of_hand_selected_text_segments
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify by human coding the specific sentences/segments where commenters suggest policy changes, then apply computational tools to link those segments to changes in policy text.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Humans are adept at identifying the relevant sentences (e.g., suggested textual edits); targeted computational linking (text reuse, phrase match) on those segments yields better measures of lobbying success than using entire comment text and helps mitigate NLP issues like negation.

rubrics_metrics.name: hand_coded_metadata_to_avoid_nlp_errors
rubrics_metrics.description: Use hand-coded metadata (e.g., pro/con position) to supplement computational methods and avoid natural language processing failures with semantics such as negation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Incorporate simple human-coded fields to disambiguate sentiment and intent before using automated linking or classification so that downstream models are less likely to misinterpret negated or complex phrasing.

rubrics_metrics.name: study_agency_processing_through_consultant_summaries_and_instructions
rubrics_metrics.description: Obtain and analyze agency instructions to consultants and the summaries consultants produce (via FOIA) to study how agencies process public comments and filter political information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consultant instructions and produced summaries provide systematic evidence of what agencies attend to; variation in tagging (e.g., 'Mass comment - organization unknown') can be used as leverage to assess the extent of agency processing and awareness of organized campaigns.

rubrics_metrics.name: use_variation_in_agency_tagging_as_processing_signal
rubrics_metrics.description: Use variation in how agencies tag or record comments (e.g., 'Mass comment - organization unknown', or tagging some identical comments as organization-associated and others not) as an observable signal of agency processing capacity and awareness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare near-identical comments that receive different tags to infer whether agencies or consultants recognized organizational sponsorship; use this to assess whether explicitly associated campaigns have different influence than untagged ones.

rubrics_metrics.name: heuristic_for_inference_about_motive_from_lobbying_effort_scale
rubrics_metrics.description: Interpret small investments in sophisticated lobbying relative to the scale of public organizing as a potential indicator that an organization primarily mobilized supporters for reasons other than influencing policy (or perceives the fight as more political than technical).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a heuristic to flag extreme cases; it does not fully address dependence on expected probability of success but may help identify campaigns mobilized for reasons other than the specific policy outcome.

rubrics_metrics.name: transparency_requirements_for_organizations
rubrics_metrics.description: Require disclosure from organizations about membership, funding, decision-making processes, methods for gathering petition signatures, and how much was spent mobilizing the public.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Transparency helps guard against astroturf and fraud and provides denominators to gauge public enthusiasm. Require disclosure of sources of funding for comments and campaigns and of whether actors acted in an organizational (paid) capacity versus individual capacity.

rubrics_metrics.name: authentication_of_comments
rubrics_metrics.description: Implement authentication procedures (e.g., email/phone/text confirmation) for comments, potentially sampling comments for verification to detect fraud and indicate stronger preferences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authentication raises participation costs but can (1) reduce identity-theft/fake signatures, (2) provide a stronger signal of intensity from authenticated comments, and (3) allow detection of fraudulent complaints if opponents try to game the system. Consider balancing stronger authentication (texts) with lower-barrier options (email) given tradeoffs.

rubrics_metrics.name: lower_barriers_to_participation_and_structuring_input
rubrics_metrics.description: Reduce costs and broaden access by structuring comment input: allow commenters to self-identify topics/sections, permit track-changes/marked-up draft submissions, offer org-provided answers for co-signing, and allow organizations to petition to add menu topics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Technology can help link comments to specific questions or sections to improve interpretability. Allowing co-signing of organizational answers or upvoting can simplify participation and reduce agency interpretation costs, but recognize tradeoffs (e.g., codifying existing mass-comment dynamics).

rubrics_metrics.name: use_polling_or_upvoting_as_reform_options (with caveats)
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider making comment periods more like polls or adding upvoting features to capture public sentiment in a representative or aggregated manner.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Representative polling can provide useful political information for some rules but has caveats (question wording, latent opinions). Upvoting codifies existing mass-comment dynamics; both approaches change the nature of deliberation and should be applied with awareness of their limitations.

rubrics_metrics.name: reduce_processing_costs_through_technology_and_question_parsing
rubrics_metrics.description: Adopt technologies that allow agencies to identify categories/topics when submitting comments, parse comment answers tied to agency questions, and accept machine-friendly formats (e.g., marked-up drafts) to lower interpretation costs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The ABA recommends allowing commenters to select categories; agencies should permit adding topics and encourage organizations to mobilize around specific question-answers. Improvements in parsing will enable more efficient extraction of political information from large volumes of comments.
